introFa: کتاب «Seven and a Half Lessons About the Brain» نوشته Lisa Feldman Barrett یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح B2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.

واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.

content: Abstract The parameters for optimal regeneration of seven commercial strawberry cultivars were tested using a range of explants and culture conditions. Efficient levels of regeneration – those needed to carry out transformation experiments – with the cultivars Calypso, Pegasus, Bole- ro, Tango and Emily were achieved with leaf discs, peti- oles, roots and stipules. Regeneration from cv. Elsanta proved to be difficult from all explant material, although unpollinated ovaries proved to be a promising explant source, with 12% of the explants regenerating shoots. In cv. Eros, regeneration occurred only from root tissue. A comparison of the genetic background suggests that there is a strong genetic component amongst the different culti- vars determining their regeneration capacity. The develop- ment of these regeneration systems provides a means to use almost the whole stock plant for the efficient genetic transformation of commercial strawberry varieties. Keywords Strawberry · Fragaria × ananassa Duch. · Adventitious shoot regeneration · In vitro culture · Explant type Abbreviations BA: N6-Benzyladenine · 2,4-D: 2,4-Dichlorophenoxyacetic acid · GA3: Gibberellin A3 · IBA: Indole-3-butyric acid · NAA: α-Naphthaleneacetic acid · TDZ: 1-Phenyl-3-(1,2,3-thiadiazol-5-yl) urea (thidiazuron) Introduction A necessary precondition for the genetic modification of commercial strawberry varieties is an efficient regenera- tion system (James et al. 1988) that would provide the means for recovering genetically modified plants follow- ing the treatment of explants with Agrobacterium or par- ticle bombardment. To date, adventitious shoot regenera- tion has been demonstrated from a variety of in vitro cul- tured explants of the cultivated strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa Duch.). These include leaf explants (Jones et al. 1988; Lui and Sandford 1988; Nehra et al. 1989; Sorvari et al. 1993), petioles (Foucault and Letouze 1987; Rugini and Orlando 1992), stipules (Rugini and Orlando 1992), stem tissue (Graham et al. 1995), runner tissue (Liu and Sandford 1988), the peduncular base of the flower bud (Foucault and Letouze 1987), mesophyll protoplasts (Nyman and Wallin 1988), anther cultures (Owen and Miller 1996), roots (Rugini and Orlando 1992) and immature embryos (Wang et al. 1984). Genetic modification is a particularly attractive means of pyramiding genes in existing commercially successful cultivars without compromising those characteristics re- quired for commercial success. Previous work in our lab- oratory has demonstrated the genetic modification of strawberry leaf explants following co-cultivation with Agrobacterium tumefaciens containing a binary transfor- mation vector (James et al. 1990). The current report describes the conditions required for the successful regeneration of shoots from a variety of explants from seven commercial strawberry cultivars. Materials and methods Establishment of cultivars in in vitro culture Strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa Duch.) cultivars Calypso, Pega- sus, Bolero, Tango, Emily and Eros, developed in the HRI, East Malling strawberry breeding programme (D. Simpson personal communication), and Elsanta were established in culture using the following method. Runner tips were collected from glasshouse- grown stock plants and washed under running tap water for 30 min to remove surface contaminants. The tips were sterilized in 10% (v/v) Domestos (0.525% sodium hypochlorite; Diversey Lever), for 20 min and then rinsed six times in sterile distilled wa- ter. binocular microscope (×6 final magnification) and placed onto strawberry proliferation media S5 in Coulter pots (Alpha Labora- tories). S5 medium consisted of MS basal medium (Murashige and Skoog 1962) (Imperial Laboratories, Andover) supplemented with 3% sucrose and the growth substances listed in Table 1. The medi- um was adjusted to pH 5.7 with 0.1 M NaOH, solidified with 0.75% Oxoid Agar No. 3 (Fisher Scientific, Loughborough) and autoclaved for 15 min at 121°C and 103 kN m–2. The in vitro cul- tures were maintained in a growth chamber at 25°C under a 16/8-h (day/night) photoperiod, with light provided by Philips MCFE flu- orescent tubes at an intensity of 14 W m–2 at the surface of the cul- ture vessel. Proliferating shoots were subcultured at 3-week inter- vals on S5 media to provide enough material to initiate regenera- tion experiments. Regeneration experiments Adventitious shoot regeneration experiments were carried out using a range of explants taken from in vitro-rooted shoot cultures 4–8 weeks after rooting. To initiate root formation, we placed the shoots on rooting media R13 (Table 1) in glass (honey) jars for 3 days under the growth conditions described above. The shoots were then transferred to medium R37 (Table 1) in glass (honey) jars for root elongation. Four types of explant – leaf discs, petioles, sti- pules and root segments – were taken from the rooted cultures. Leaf discs were cut from newly expanded leaves using a size-2 cork bor- er, giving 7-mm-diameter discs. The discs were cultured with the abaxial surface in contact with the regeneration media. Entire roots and petioles were cut with a scalpel into 1-cm explants. Stipule ex- plants were cut carefully to avoid including axillary buds. In addition to the in vitro explants, pre-pollination ovaries, from unopened flowers, were collected from plants in the glass- house 3–4 days before anthesis. The flower buds were sterilized by immersion in 5% (v/v) Domestos for 10 min, then rinsed six times in sterile distilled water. The petals, sepals and anthers were then removed, exposing the ovaries on the receptacle. The ovaries were removed from the surface of the receptacle and viewed under a binocular microscope (×6 magnification) using a scalpel to dis- lodge the ovaries and a curved jeweler’s forceps to transfer them to the surface of the media. The transfer was facilitated by grasp- ing the style with the forceps to avoid damage to the ovaries. Regeneration experiments were carried out on MS media con- taining various combinations of the growth substances BA, 2,4-D, NAA and TDZ (Table 1). Explants were placed into 9-cm petri dishes containing 30 ml of media and cultured in a growth cham- ber maintained at 25°C and a 16/8-h (day/night) photoperiod. Results and discussion The strawberry cultivars used in this investigation were chosen on the basis of being the most commercially suc- cessful varieties currently grown in the UK that have been released from the East Malling strawberry breed- ing programme. In addition to the East Malling culti- vars, cv. Elsanta was selected for two reasons: it is the most economically important cultivar currently grown in Northern Europe, and it has many characteristics that could be improved in a genetic modification pro- gramme. In order to establish an efficient transformation system for each cultivar, we considered it necessary to test the efficiency of regeneration from all parts of the plant available for experimental use. Combinations of re- generation media were based on those previously devel- oped in our laboratory for the regeneration of strawberry cv. Rapella (James et al. 1990) and apple cv. Green- sleeves (James et al. 1993). Effect of explant type Callus formation and subsequent adventitious shoot pro- duction were observed on leaf discs (Fig. 1), petioles, stipules and roots, within 3–4 weeks of their transfer on- to regeneration media. For the majority of cultivars test- ed, leaf discs gave the highest percentage of regenera- tion, with maximal regeneration occurring with cvs. Calypso and Tango (Table 2). oles was most effective in Tango and Emily, where over 90% of the explants produced shoots. Stipules proved to be a good source of explant material for regeneration with Tango, Pegasus, Calypso and Emily, all of which exhibited a regeneration efficiency of 60% or more. High levels (>than 60%) of regeneration from roots were observed in Calypso, Pegasus, Bolero, Tango and Emily, with the most efficient cultivar being Emily. In contrast, regeneration frequencies were relatively low in all of the explant material from Elsanta and Eros. With this in mind and considering the commercial dominance of Elsanta in the European market place, pre-pollination ovaries of Elsanta were tested as a potential explant source; a regeneration frequency of 12% was achieved with this material. Effect of growth substance combinations in media Various combinations of the cytokinin BA, the thidi- azole-substituted phenylurea TDZ, (Huetteman and Preece 1993) and the auxins NAA and 2,4-D were tested to determine their effect on regeneration from a range of explant types and cultivars. For leaf discs of Calypso, Emily, Bolero and Elsanta, a combination of 1 mg l–1 TDZ and 0.2 mg l–1 2,4-D, (me- dium ZD102) was found to be the most efficient, whereas for Pegasus and Tango 2 mg l–1 BA, 0.5 mg l–1 TDZ and 0.2 mg l–1 2,4-D, (medium K1) gave the highest levels of regeneration. Medium K1 gave optimal regeneration for Pegasus and Tango for all of the explant types tested. For Calypso, media supplemented with a combination of 1 mg l–1 TDZ and 0.2 mg l–1 NAA (ZN102) was better than those containing 2,4-D for obtaining regeneration from petioles, stipules, and roots. The media K2, contain- ing 2 mg l–1 BA and 0.2 mg l–1 2,4-D, was optimal for obtaining regeneration from roots of Emily and stimulat- ed shoot regeneration from roots of the more recalcitrant cultivars Elsanta, Eros, and Bolero. Effect of cultivar Whereas Calypso, Pegasus, Tango and Emily regenerat- ed efficiently from all of the explant types tested, Elsanta and the related cultivar Eros were more recalcitrant. Bolero was intermediate with respect to regeneration ca- pacity. We conducted 19 regeneration experiments over a pe- riod of 2 years with Elsanta using a range of explants and growth regulator combinations and achieved a maxi- mum of 4% regeneration. Elsanta and Eros (data not shown) often produced adventitious roots in treatments where high levels of shoot formation occurred in the other cultivars tested. These results suggest that a high level of endogenous auxin may be present which pre- vents shoot regeneration (Cassells 1979). In comparing the parentage of different varieties with frequencies of regeneration, we found indications of a genetic linkage to recalcitrance. The regeneration of Elsanta and Eros appears to have a genetic basis, with Eros having Elsanta as a maternal parent (Fig. 2a). This genetic effect was also apparent with the highly regener- ative cultivars Calypso and Tango, which are both the re- sult of crosses between the easy-to-regenerate cultivar Rapella (James et al. 1990) and Selva (Fig. 2b). Rugini and Orlando (1992) reported that Gea, one of the parents of Emily, was the most regenerative of the cultivars that they tested, and Emily showed prolific regeneration rates in our investigation (Fig. 2c). Similarly, the high levels of regeneration exhibited by Pegasus (Fig. 2d) were matched by the maternal parent Redgauntlet, as reported by Jones et al. (1988). A number of additional experiments were carried out with Elsanta in an attempt to increase the efficiency of regeneration. These were mainly designed to change 399 Fig. 1 a Leaf-disc regeneration (explants from cv. Calypso shown as example). i leaf-disc explant, ii callus formation on medium ZD102 after 14 days in culture, iii shoot regeneration from callus after 42 days, iv shoot excised from leaf disc and transferred to proliferation medium S5 for 14 days. b Calypso leaf discs show- ing 100% of explants forming shoots following 42 days of culture on media ZD102

either the availability or the type of growth substance in the regeneration media. The experiments (details not shown) included reducing auxin levels in relation to cy- tokinin or TDZ concentrations, providing a 4-day auxin/ cytokinin pulse before transferring explants to auxin-free media, using the diphenyl urea CPPU that has powerful cytokinin effects in other species (Mohamed et al. 1992), pre-chilling of stock material at 4°C to enhance subse- quent shoot regeneration (Negrutiu and Jacobs 1978) and testing the effect of light and dark treatments both on the stock material to induce etiolation (Jagannathan and Marcotrigiano 1986), and on the explants during the re- generation period (Welander 1988). These experiments failed to significantly increase the levels of regeneration. For Agrobacterium-mediated gene transfer technolo- gy to be applied to genetically improve existing commer- cial strawberry cultivars, it is essential that efficient re- generation systems are available for every cultivar to be modified. Our investigation demonstrated that it is possi- ble to obtain efficient regeneration levels (>90%) for the commercial cultivars Calypso, Pegasus, Emily and Tango. In contrast, Elsanta and Eros were more recalci- trant. This variation in the ability to regenerate adventi- tious shoots from different strawberry cultivars has been observed previously by Jones et al. (1988) and Nehra et al. (1989). These investigators observed that difficulty in regeneration of cultivars when cultured in vitro was linked with the production of phenolics in the media, darker green leaves and root systems containing antho- cyanin. The high levels of regeneration we obtained from leaf discs (100% with Calypso and Tango) compares well with the 79% reported for cv. Redcoat by Nehra et al. (1989) and the 85.4% for Jonsok reported by Sorvari et al. (1993). Our results for regeneration from petioles were 92% for Tango and Emily compared to 16% with cv. Gea, observed by Rugini and Orlando (1992). These workers obtained up to 96% shoot regeneration from sti- pules, whereas we achieved 98% with Tango. To date, the ability to regenerate shoots from strawberry root sys- tems has only been reported by Rugini and Orlando (1992), who obtained 16% regeneration with Gea. The present study indicates that roots can be an important ex- plant source for transformation work as up to 98% of the roots formed shoots in cv. Emily. Our results show that all parts of the root are capable of regeneration, which means that it is possible to harvest up to 30 root explants per rooted shoot. The most successful explant tested for regeneration of Elsanta was the pre-pollination ovary. Previous unpub- lished work in this laboratory in which these ovaries were used as explants for adventitious shoot regeneration gave the following percentage regeneration results: Rapella (21%), Hapil (30%), Brighton (53%) and Cam- bridge Favourite (60%). The use of this explant source for the difficult-to-regenerate Elsanta may prove useful in future transformation experiments with this economi- cally important cultivar. Elsanta pre-pollination ovaries provided an abundant supply of explants (up to 300 per flower) that were low in phenolic compounds and did not produce adventitious roots on callus in vitro. These factors were observed in the other explants tested, and this observation may be the key to the relative success in adventitious shoot growth obtained with these explants. Moreover, on the basis of anatomical studies we have es- tablished that ovaries selected for tissue culture at this immature stage (tight green bud) do not contain embryo sacs and are composed of nucellar cells and ovary wall tissues. This should mean that any variations in pheno- type observed in regenerated plants would be due to so- 400 Fig. 2a–d Comparison of re- generation frequencies using inheritance charts of the culti- vars. a Eros/Elsanta, b Calypso/ Tango, c Emily, d Pegasus. Figure shows percentage regen- eration from leaf explants and the source of the data. Percent- ages are based on 50 leaf discs per treatment for the present work and on at least 20 discs per treatment in previously cited investigations

maclonal variation and not to meiosis and segregation of characters. Efficient adventitious shoot regeneration has been demonstrated for the commercial strawberry cultivars Calypso, Pegasus, Bolero, Tango and Emily, using a range of explants. It will now be possible to use leaf, root, petiole and stipules from in vitro-grown plants as source material for Agrobacterium tumefaciens-mediated transformation experiments with these cultivars. Elsanta and Eros proved to be difficult to regenerate, and more extensive experimental work needs to be carried out on these cultivars before genetic modification experiments can proceed. The abundance of pre-pollination ovaries at certain times of the year combined with the speed and ease of excision could make this type of explant the best choice for the development of regeneration systems in otherwise recalcitrant cultivars. The investigation described here suggests that regener- ation frequencies may be determined genetically. Thus, when selecting cultivars to undergo genetic modification, it may be worthwhile to have a basic knowledge of the ge- netic background and its effect on regeneration. It would be of interest, possibly by use of DNA markers, to deter- mine the genetic basis of recalcitrance to regeneration.
